Epidemiology & Risk Factors.title: Prostate Cancer Epidemiology & Risk Factors
Epidemiology & Risk Factors.html:
Prostate cancer is the most common cancer you'll see in men, and a large share of any radiation oncology clinic. The central theme: it is extremely common, but most men who have it won't die of it. That tension drives everything about screening, risk grouping, and how aggressively we treat. This page answers one question: who has prostate cancer, and which cancers matter?

How Common Is Prostate Cancer?

1 in 8

Lifetime risk for a US man. The most common cancer in men (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer).

#2 cause of death

The 2nd most common cause of cancer death in men, after lung cancer.

Mostly curable

Most men are diagnosed with localized disease, where 5-year survival is nearly 100%. Many cancers are slow-growing and never become life-threatening.

Very common, often indolent. The job is to find and treat the cancers that matter, and leave alone the ones that don't.

Risk Is Not the Same as Aggressiveness

Two different questions get called "risk" in prostate cancer. Keep them apart and the rest of the module gets easier.

Before diagnosis
Risk of developing prostate cancer
  • Age
  • Family history
  • Black ancestry
  • Germline mutations (BRCA2 and others)

Decides who should be screened, and how early.

After diagnosis
Risk that this cancer will progress
  • PSA
  • Grade Group
  • Clinical T stage
  • Extent of disease on biopsy and imaging

Becomes the NCCN risk group (Workup & Staging), which frames treatment.

Who Gets Prostate Cancer? Risk Factors

1
Age

The strongest risk factor. Rare before 40; most men are diagnosed in their 60s. Autopsy studies find cancer in a large share of older men who died of something else.

2
Black Ancestry

Black men have a higher incidence, are diagnosed younger, and have about twice the mortality of White men, a disparity driven by both biology and access to care.

3
Family History

A father or brother with prostate cancer roughly doubles the risk, more with several relatives or diagnosis at a young age.

4
Germline Mutations

BRCA2 is the most important (more aggressive disease). Others include BRCA1, ATM, CHEK2, HOXB13, and Lynch syndrome genes.

  • Other factors have weaker evidence (obesity, diet, smoking). BPH does not cause prostate cancer.
  • Histology: over 95% are adenocarcinoma (acinar). Rare variants (ductal, small cell/neuroendocrine) behave worse and may not make PSA.

Why Does Genetics Matter to a Radiation Oncologist?

You don't need to memorize the gene list. You need to know what a germline finding changes:

A germline mutation can change…Example
How aggressive the disease is likely to beBRCA2 carriers present younger with higher-grade disease, so active surveillance is approached more cautiously
Family counselingRelatives may need earlier screening (prostate, breast, ovarian, pancreatic cancer)
Systemic treatment optionsBRCA2/ATM and other repair-gene mutations open the door to PARP inhibitors in advanced disease; mismatch repair defects to immunotherapy
Future treatment planningThe result follows the patient into recurrence and metastatic decisions

Germline testing is recommended for men with high-risk, very high-risk, node-positive, or metastatic disease, and for anyone with a strong family history.

Clinical Pearl

A young man with high-grade prostate cancer and a family history of breast, ovarian, or pancreatic cancer should make you think BRCA2. Refer for germline testing: it affects his family and his treatment options.

Clinical Presentation: Usually Silent

Localized prostate cancer is usually asymptomatic. Most cancers today are found because a PSA came back high, not because of symptoms.

PresentationWhat it suggests
Raised PSA, normal examThe usual story: cT1c disease
Nodule or induration on DREPalpable tumor, cT2 or higher (usually peripheral zone)
Frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream (LUTS)Usually BPH, not cancer; can mean locally advanced disease
Hematuria, hematospermiaLess common; nonspecific
Bone pain, back pain, leg weaknessBone metastases or spinal cord compression (an emergency)

An Elevated PSA Is Not a Diagnosis

PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is made by normal and cancerous prostate tissue. It's a test of prostate activity, not of cancer. PSA can rise from:

Benign enlargement

BPH: a bigger gland makes more PSA.

Inflammation / infection

Prostatitis, UTI, urinary retention.

Recent instrumentation

Biopsy, catheter, cystoscopy (and recent ejaculation).

Prostate cancer

Only one of the possibilities.

So the durable pathway after a high PSA is:

1
Repeat / confirm the PSA
→
2
Risk assessment
→
3
Prostate MRI ± biomarkers
→
4
Biopsy if concerning
  • 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) roughly halve the PSA. Double the value to interpret it.
  • PSA kinetics matter most after a diagnosis or treatment: a short PSA doubling time after surgery or RT points to a more aggressive recurrence (Treatment Paradigms).
Further risk stratification: PSA density, free PSA, and biomarkers▾

These tools help decide who needs an MRI or biopsy. Know what they are; you won't be quizzed on cutoffs on rounds.

ToolWhat it isPoints toward cancer when
PSA densityPSA ÷ prostate volume (MRI or ultrasound)Higher density, often above about 0.15 ng/mL/cc
Free/total PSACancer makes relatively more bound PSALower free fraction
Blood and urine biomarkers4Kscore, PHI, urine testsHigher scores; used to select men for biopsy
Self-check: PSA 6.0 in a man on finasteride. What's the "real" PSA?▾

About 12. 5-alpha reductase inhibitors lower PSA by roughly half, so double it. That's a meaningfully high PSA worth confirming and working up.

PSA Screening: Weighing Benefit Against Harm

Benefit
What screening does
  • Finds cancer earlier
  • ERSPC: lowers prostate cancer mortality (~20% relative) and fewer men present with metastases
Harm
What it costs
  • No clear drop in overall mortality
  • Overdiagnosis and overtreatment of indolent cancers
  • Biopsy complications (infection, bleeding)
  • Treatment side effects (incontinence, erectile dysfunction, bowel toxicity)
Screening should be individualized through shared decision-making, with earlier discussion for men at increased risk because of age, family history, Black ancestry, or germline susceptibility.

Active surveillance for low-risk cancers has made screening much safer: finding a GG1 cancer no longer means treating it.

Reference: current guideline screening ages (check before using)▾

Screening guidance is actively revised (the AUA/SUO Early Detection guideline was amended in 2026). As of that version:

  • Increased risk (Black ancestry, germline mutation, strong family history): offer screening starting at about 40–45.
  • Average risk: shared decision-making, with 55–69 the core group in most guidelines (USPSTF grade C).
  • Older men or limited life expectancy: routine screening is not recommended.
  • PSA is the first test; a newly elevated PSA is repeated before biomarkers, imaging, or biopsy.
High-Yield Summary

Anatomy & Lymphatics.title: Prostate Anatomy, TRUS & Lymph Nodes
Anatomy & Lymphatics.html:
Prostate anatomy answers three questions: where in the gland is the cancer (which zone, base or apex), what is right next to it (the rectum, bladder, urethra, and other organs that shape the plan), and where does it drain (the pelvic nodes that decide N stage and the elective RT field). Every piece of anatomy here comes back later as a target or an organ at risk. Learn the structures on drawings here; the Imaging section shows them on MRI, CT, and ultrasound.

The Prostate: Main Regions

The Zones (McNeal)

ZoneWhereShare of cancersWhat to remember
Peripheral (PZ)Posterior and lateral, against the rectum~70%What the DRE feels. Tumor here is close to the rectum and the neurovascular bundles.
Transition (TZ)Around the urethra~20%Where BPH grows.
Central (CZ)Around the ejaculatory ducts at the base~5–10%Less common; near the seminal vesicles.
Anterior fibromuscular stromaFront of the glandNon-glandularAnterior tumors are missed by DRE; MRI finds them.
Cancer lives in the Peripheral zone (next to the rectum). BPH lives in the Transition zone (around the urethra).

Base, Mid-Gland, Apex

  • Base: the top, under the bladder neck. The seminal vesicles attach here, so tumor at the base is the route to SV invasion.
  • Mid-gland: the bulk of the peripheral zone.
  • Apex: the bottom tip, above the external sphincter. Hard to see on CT (MRI fusion helps) and the most common site of a positive surgical margin.

How the Cancer Grows Out of the Gland

Local extension follows the anatomy, and each step changes both the stage and what the radiation has to cover.

1
Confined to the gland
→
2
Through the capsule (EPE), often posterolateral at the nerve bundles
→
3
Into the seminal vesicles from the base
→
4
Bladder neck, rectum, pelvic side wall

As the cancer reaches further, the target grows: prostate alone, then prostate plus a margin for extension, then the seminal vesicles, and for higher-risk disease the pelvic nodes.

The Neighbors: Organs at Risk

Rectum

Directly behind the prostate, separated by Denonvilliers' fascia. One of the principal dose-limiting organs: proctitis and bleeding.

Bladder

Above the base. Treated comfortably full to push bowel away and spare bladder wall. Frequency, urgency, hematuria.

Urethra

Runs through the gland, so it can't be avoided. Urethral dose drives urinary symptoms, especially after brachy and SBRT.

Neurovascular Bundles & Penile Bulb

Bundles run posterolaterally (5 and 7 o'clock). The penile bulb sits below the apex. Both relate to erectile function.

Small Bowel / Sigmoid

Matters most when the pelvic nodes are treated. A full bladder helps keep it out.

Femoral Heads

Lateral to the pelvis. Kept low to avoid fracture or necrosis.

Which organ limits a given plan depends on the technique and the volume: the rectum for the prostate itself, the urethra and bladder for brachy and SBRT, and the bowel once the pelvic nodes are added.

Rectal spacer

A hydrogel spacer injected into the space between the prostate and the anterior rectal wall increases the physical separation between them, which can reduce rectal dose in selected patients. It is an adjunct, not a requirement for prostate RT.

Self-check: on MRI a tumor bulges through the posterolateral capsule at 7 o'clock. What does that mean, and which structure is at risk?▾

Extraprostatic extension, right where the neurovascular bundle runs. A surgeon would likely not spare that bundle, and the radiation target needs to cover the extension.

The Lymph Nodes: Drainage and Staging

Lymph from the prostate travels laterally to the pelvic side wall, then up along the iliac vessels.

1
Obturator + internal iliac
→
2
External iliac + presacral
→
3
Common iliac
→
4
Para-aortic

Regional vs Distant

Node groupWhereAJCC
ObturatorPelvic side wall, along the obturator vesselsN1
Internal iliac (hypogastric)Deep pelvis, along the internal iliac vesselsN1
External iliacPelvic brim, along the external iliac vesselsN1
Sacral (presacral, lateral sacral)In front of the sacrumN1
Common iliacAbove the bifurcationM1a
Para-aortic, inguinal, supraclavicularOutside the pelvisM1a
Inside the true pelvis = N1 (stage IVA, still treated for cure). Common iliac and above, or inguinal = M1a.

The Elective Pelvic Nodal Field: What You Should Know

When the pelvic nodes are treated electively, the volume generally covers the obturator, internal iliac, external iliac, and presacral regions, plus the distal common iliac nodes. Who gets it is a Treatment Paradigms question: it depends on the estimated risk of occult nodal disease, not on anatomy.

Planning details: contouring the pelvic nodes▾

Resident-level reference, based on the RTOG/NRG pelvic nodal consensus. You won't be expected to know these on a sub-I.

  • The volume is built around the vessels with a margin of roughly 7 mm, trimmed off bowel, bladder, and bone.
  • The superior border is usually around L5/S1 (distal common iliac).
  • Presacral coverage typically runs over the upper sacrum (about S1–S3).
  • The external iliac nodes stop near the top of the femoral heads, and the obturator nodes near the top of the pubic symphysis.
Historical / planning pearl: the Roach formula▾

Estimated risk of nodal involvement = (2/3 × PSA) + [(Gleason score − 6) × 10]. For PSA 18 and Gleason 4+4: 12 + 20 = about 32%.

The Roach formula historically estimated nodal involvement and helped guide pelvic nodal RT decisions; contemporary practice also incorporates MRI, PSMA PET, Grade Group, clinical stage, and guideline-based risk assessment. Treat it as a quick estimate, not a decision rule.

High-Yield Summary

Imaging.title: Prostate Imaging: MRI, CT, PSMA PET & Bone Scan
Imaging.html:
Imaging plays three different roles in prostate cancer. MRI looks inside the gland: it finds the tumor, guides the biopsy, and shows whether it has broken out. PSMA PET and bone scan look outside: have the nodes or bones been reached? Then the planning CT is where the radiation plan is built. For each scan, ask: what does this image tell me?

ModalityThe question it answersWhen you'll see it
mpMRI prostateIs there a significant tumor? Where? Has it left the gland?Before biopsy, for staging, surveillance, and planning
PSMA PET/CTAre there nodal or bone metastases? Where is the recurrence?Higher-risk staging; rising PSA after treatment; planning
Bone scan (± CT A/P)Are there bone metastases?The conventional alternative to PSMA PET
CT simulation (fused with MRI)Where exactly do we aim, and what do we avoid?Every external beam plan
TRUSWhere is the gland during a biopsy or implant?Biopsy and brachytherapy

Multiparametric MRI

What Each Sequence Is For

SequenceWhat it's for
T2-weightedAnatomy, transition zone lesions, and local extension (EPE, SVI). Cancer is a dark focus.
DWI / ADCThe most important sequence for peripheral zone lesions. Cancer restricts diffusion (dark on ADC).
DCE (contrast)A limited, tie-breaking role in PI-RADS; useful in some recurrence settings.

PI-RADS: How Suspicious Is It?

PI-RADS is a standardized 1–5 score for the likelihood of clinically significant cancer.

PI-RADSMeaningUsual next step
1–2Significant cancer unlikelyOften no biopsy (PSA density and risk help decide)
3EquivocalBiopsy depends on PSA density and other risk factors
4–5Likely / highly likelyTargeted biopsy

Local Extension on MRI

Extraprostatic extension
Through the capsule
  • Capsular bulge or irregularity
  • Broad tumor–capsule contact
  • Neurovascular bundle asymmetry
Seminal vesicle invasion
Into the SVs
  • Dark T2 tissue filling the normally bright SV
  • Direct spread from a base tumor

These findings change the radiation plan (SV coverage, margins, ADT, sometimes nodes) and are weighed in the overall risk assessment.

MRI Changes Biopsy and Planning, Not the Clinical T Stage by Itself

NCCN risk grouping uses the clinical T stage from the DRE. A 2 cm PI-RADS 5 lesion in a gland that feels normal is still cT1c, not cT2. The MRI directs the biopsy, flags extension, and shapes the radiation target, but MRI appearance does not automatically become the clinical T stage.

Self-check: a man on active surveillance for GG1 disease has a new 1.8 cm, markedly dark-on-ADC peripheral zone lesion. Next step?▾

This is a highly suspicious (PI-RADS 5) lesion, so the next step is an MRI-targeted biopsy. If it shows GG2 or higher, he's reclassified and into treatment discussions.

Pelvic Lymph Nodes on CT

  • Every pelvic node group is named for the vessel it sits next to, so find the vessel first.
  • The common iliac bifurcation is the staging line: nodes below it in the true pelvis are regional (N1); common iliac and above are distant (M1a).
  • CT only calls a node abnormal when it is enlarged, so small involved nodes are missed.

PSMA PET/CT

PSMA (prostate-specific membrane antigen) is highly expressed on most prostate cancer cells, so a PSMA tracer lights up nodes and bones that CT and bone scan would call normal.

PSMA PET has higher sensitivity for metastatic disease than CT and bone scan, but a negative scan does not exclude microscopic disease.
SettingWhat PSMA PET does
Newly diagnosed, higher-risk diseaseStaging: are the nodes or bones involved? (proPSMA: more accurate than CT + bone scan)
Rising PSA after treatmentLocalization: where is the recurrence, even at low PSA levels?
Treatment planningMay change the radiation targets: add nodes, boost a lesion, or treat a metastasis

PSMA PET Changes the Map

Same patient, rising PSA after prostatectomy:

Conventional imaging
Nothing seen outside the bed

Assumed prostate-bed recurrence → prostate-bed RT.

PSMA PET
Bed lesion + one pelvic node

Prostate bed + pelvic nodes + a boost to the PET-positive node.

  • Physiologic uptake to know: salivary and lacrimal glands, kidneys, bladder, bowel, liver, spleen, and ganglia (can mimic nodes).
  • Some aggressive or neuroendocrine tumors are PSMA-negative.
  • The trials that defined most of our treatments staged patients with conventional imaging, so interpret "PSMA-only" disease with care.

Bone Scan

  • Tc-99m bone scan shows osteoblastic metastases as hot spots, mostly in the axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs).
  • The superscan: diffuse, intense uptake with faint or absent kidneys. Looks deceptively "clean"; actually means extensive bone disease.
  • False positives: arthritis, fractures, Paget disease. CT or MRI can clarify a single uncertain spot.
  • Bone lesion counts help define volume in metastatic disease (Workup & Staging).

CT Simulation: What Happens at Prostate Simulation?

The prostate moves. The rectum and bladder change from day to day. Good preparation and image guidance make the target reproducible.

StepWhat happensWhy
Bladder preparationDrink a set volume before sim and before every treatmentA comfortably full bladder pushes bowel away and keeps the bladder in a reproducible shape
Rectal preparationEmpty rectum (bowel regimen, sometimes an enema)Gas and stool push the prostate forward and change rectal dose
ImmobilizationSupine with a leg and foot cushionSame position every day
Fiducial markers (when used)Gold seeds placed in the prostate before simVisible on daily imaging so therapists align to the prostate, not the bones
Rectal spacer (selected patients)Hydrogel placed before simMore distance between prostate and rectum
CT scanThin-slice planning CT through the pelvisThe dataset the plan is calculated on
MRI fusionPlanning MRI registered to the CTShows the prostate edges (especially the apex) and the tumor much better than CT
ContouringTargets and organs at risk are drawnDefines what gets dose and what is protected
Daily image guidanceCone-beam CT or fiducial imaging before each fractionCorrects for daily prostate motion
  • After prostatectomy, the target is the prostate bed, built around the vesicourethral anastomosis and bladder neck using a consensus atlas.

The Transrectal Ultrasound (TRUS) View: What You'll See in the Brachy Suite

During a prostate brachytherapy implant, the patient is in lithotomy, a TRUS probe sits in the rectum, and needles go through the perineum via a template grid. You'll be looking at this screen for an hour, and you may be asked to name what's on it. (What the procedure is for is in Treatment Paradigms.)

How to Orient Yourself

Transverse (axial)
Like a CT slice
  • Bottom of the screen = rectum/probe; top = anterior (pubic bone)
  • The urethra (Foley) is near the center: a bright ring or dot
  • The grid dots match the perineal template (letters across, numbers up)
  • The physicist steps through planes from base to apex
Sagittal (longitudinal)
Side view
  • Bladder (black fluid) and the Foley balloon mark the base
  • The apex is at the other end
  • Used to check needle depth
  • Rectum/probe is still at the bottom

Things You Might Be Asked

  • "Why do we care about the urethra?" Too much dose near it causes retention and urinary toxicity, so plans limit urethral dose.
  • "Why the rectum?" It sits right on the probe; seeds or hot spots near the anterior rectal wall raise the risk of rectal bleeding.
  • "Who's a poor brachy candidate?" A large gland (pubic arch interference), a prior TURP defect, or significant urinary symptoms at baseline.
High-Yield Summary

Workup & Staging.title: Prostate Cancer Workup, Gleason & Staging
Workup & Staging.html:
This page answers one question: how do I turn a PSA into a treatment-ready diagnosis? Prostate staging confuses people because three systems are stacked on top of each other: the Grade Group (how aggressive it looks), the TNM stage (how far it has spread), and the NCCN risk group (which combines them with PSA). This page builds them in the order you'd meet them for a real patient, then adds the step people forget: is this patient likely to benefit from curative treatment? The NCCN workup and full AJCC tables are at the bottom of the page.

1
PSA + DRE
→
2
MRI → biopsy
→
3
Grade Group
→
4
T stage
→
5
NCCN risk group
→
6
Imaging for N and M
→
7
Life expectancy + patient factors

Step 1–2: From a High PSA to a Diagnosis

  1. PSA (repeat it) and a DRE. The DRE sets the clinical T stage.
  2. Prostate MRI before biopsy. Suspicious lesions get targeted.
  3. Biopsy: MRI-targeted cores + systematic cores, increasingly transperineal (lower infection risk than transrectal).
  4. The pathology report gives the Grade Group, number of positive cores (e.g., 4 of 12), how much of each core is involved, and adverse features such as cribriform pattern or intraductal carcinoma.

Step 3: Gleason Score and Grade Group

The pathologist grades the gland architecture as pattern 3 (well-formed glands), 4 (poorly formed or fused), or 5 (no glands). The Gleason score adds the most common pattern to the next most common, and the Grade Group turns that into a simple 1–5 scale:

Gleason scoreGrade Group
3+3=6GG1
3+4=7GG2
4+3=7GG3
8 (4+4, 3+5, 5+3)GG4
9–10GG5
3+4 and 4+3 are both Gleason 7 but are not biologically equivalent. The first number is the dominant pattern, so 4+3 (GG3) behaves worse than 3+4 (GG2).
  • Always identify the highest Grade Group present, but also pay attention to how much of the biopsy is involved and whether adverse patterns such as cribriform or intraductal carcinoma are present.
Pathology nuances: patterns, tertiary grade, and why "6" is the lowest▾
  • Patterns 1 and 2 are no longer assigned on biopsies, so the lowest score you'll see is 3+3=6. That's why Grade Groups were introduced: "6 out of 10" sounds intermediate, but it is the lowest grade.
  • On biopsy, a small amount of a higher pattern still counts: mostly 3 with some 4 and a little 5 is reported as 3+5=8.
  • Pattern 3: small, separate, round glands. Pattern 4: fused, cribriform, or poorly formed glands. Pattern 5: solid sheets, cords, single cells, or comedonecrosis.

Step 4: Clinical T Stage (by DRE)

cTWhat it means
T1cFound on needle biopsy for a raised PSA; not palpable. The most common T stage today.
T2a / T2b / T2cPalpable and confined: ≤half of one lobe / >half of one lobe / both lobes
T3aExtraprostatic extension
T3bSeminal vesicle invasion
T4Fixed or invading bladder, rectum, external sphincter, levators, or pelvic wall
  • T1 vs T2 is about the finger, not the size. A big tumor that can't be felt is still T1c, even if the MRI shows it clearly.
  • Pathologic T (after prostatectomy) has no T1 and no T2 subdivisions: pT2, pT3a, pT3b, pT4.
Quick check: PSA 7, normal DRE, MRI shows a 2 cm PI-RADS 5 lesion confined to the gland. What's the cT stage?▾

cT1c. Clinical T stage for NCCN risk grouping comes from the DRE, and the tumor isn't palpable. The MRI lesion guides the biopsy and planning, but doesn't make it T2.

Step 5: The NCCN Risk Groups

The risk group combines T stage, Grade Group, and PSA (plus core involvement and PSA density at the extremes) to estimate how likely this cancer is to progress.

Intermediate risk factors (IRFs)

T2b–T2c · GG2 or GG3 · PSA 10–20

High-risk features

T3a · GG4 or GG5 · PSA >20

Risk groupDefinition (N0 M0)
Very lowT1c, GG1, PSA <10, PSA density <0.15 (and limited core involvement)
LowT1–T2a, GG1, PSA <10 (not very low)
Favorable intermediateExactly 1 IRF, GG1 or GG2, and <50% of biopsy cores positive
Unfavorable intermediate2–3 IRFs, or GG3, or ≥50% of cores positive
HighExactly 1 high-risk feature: T3a, GG4–5, or PSA >20
Very highT3b–T4, or primary Gleason pattern 5, or 2–3 high-risk features, or >4 cores with GG4–5
RegionalAny T, N1, M0
MetastaticAny T, any N, M1
Count the intermediate factors, then check for high-risk features. Seminal vesicles, primary pattern 5, or two high-risk features = very high.
Quick check: cT1c, Gleason 3+4, PSA 12, 5 of 12 cores. Favorable or unfavorable?▾

Unfavorable intermediate. Two IRFs (GG2 and PSA 10–20). Favorable needs exactly one.

Quick check: cT2a, Gleason 4+4, PSA 24. High or very high?▾

Very high. Two high-risk features (GG4 and PSA >20). One would be high; two or more is very high.

Step 6: N and M, and Who Needs Staging Imaging

  • Very low, low, favorable intermediate: the chance of metastases is small, so no routine bone or body imaging.
  • Unfavorable intermediate and higher: image the bones and pelvis/abdomen, with PSMA PET/CT or conventional CT (or MRI) + bone scan.
CategoryMeaning
N0 / N1No regional nodes / regional pelvic nodes (obturator, internal and external iliac, sacral)
M1aNonregional nodes (common iliac, para-aortic, inguinal, beyond)
M1bBone
M1cOther sites (lung, liver) with or without bone

For metastatic disease, volume matters: high volume = ≥4 bone metastases with ≥1 outside the spine and pelvis, or any visceral metastasis (CHAARTED). Everything else is low volume.

AJCC Stage Is Not the NCCN Risk Group

Both appear in the chart, and they answer different questions.

AJCC stage (8th edition)
Describes anatomic extent
  • T, N, M, plus PSA and Grade Group
  • Stage I to IVB
  • Used for registries, prognosis, and communication
NCCN risk group
Treatment-oriented risk classification
  • PSA + Grade Group + clinical T stage + biopsy extent
  • Very low to very high, regional, metastatic
  • The framework for treatment decisions
AJCC stage = anatomic extent. NCCN risk group = treatment-oriented risk. A patient can be AJCC stage III and NCCN high risk at the same time; they are not interchangeable.
AJCC stage groups at a glance▾
StageCriteria
IcT1–T2a (or pT2), PSA <10, GG1
II (A–C)T1–2, PSA <20; rising Grade Group (IIB = GG2, IIC = GG3–4)
IIIAT1–2, PSA ≥20, GG1–4
IIIBT3–T4, GG1–4
IIICAny T, GG5
IVA / IVBN1 M0 / M1
Quick check: cT1c, Gleason 4+5, PSA 6, N0 M0. AJCC stage and NCCN risk group?▾

AJCC IIIC (GG5 alone makes it IIIC) and NCCN high risk (one high-risk feature, GG5; the primary pattern is 4, not 5). It shows why the two systems aren't interchangeable.

Step 7: Life Expectancy Before Treatment

Before choosing between surveillance, surgery, and radiation, ask: does this patient have enough life expectancy to benefit from curative treatment? Prostate cancer often takes many years to cause harm, so the answer can change the plan as much as the risk group does.

Longer life expectancy
Consider curative treatment

Depending on risk group: active surveillance for lower-risk disease, or definitive RT or surgery.

Limited life expectancy
Observation may be more appropriate

Watchful waiting: no curative plan, treat symptoms if they develop. Higher-risk disease may still warrant treatment.

Also record what the patient brings to the decision: baseline urinary, bowel, and sexual function, comorbidities, prostate size, prior pelvic surgery or RT, and his own priorities.

Worked Example

Worked Example
Patient

A healthy 66-year-old with PSA 8.4. DRE: firm nodule in the left lobe, less than half the lobe. MRI: 1.6 cm PI-RADS 5 left peripheral zone lesion, no extension. Biopsy: Gleason 3+4=7 in 3 of 14 cores.

Your thought process

Gleason 3+4 → GG2. Palpable, ≤half of one lobe → cT2a. PSA <10. One IRF (GG2), cores 3/14 (<50%) → favorable intermediate. No staging imaging needed. AJCC: IIB. Long life expectancy, so curative options are on the table.

Now change one thing

Biopsy instead shows 4+3=7. That's GG3 → unfavorable intermediate → now he needs staging imaging, and if he chooses radiation, short-course ADT generally enters the plan. Same tumor, two numbers flipped, a different treatment framework.

NCCN Workup by Risk Group

What the NCCN Prostate Cancer Guidelines recommend before treatment, simplified for learning. Click a tab or use the arrows. Always check the current guideline for real patients.

HistoryLife expectancy, symptoms (urinary, bowel, sexual function), family history
Exam / labsDRE, PSA, PSA density
PathologyGleason/Grade Group, number of positive cores, % core involvement
ImagingProstate MRI (ideally before biopsy)
GeneticsGermline testing if family history, high/very high risk, regional, or metastatic
Staging imagingNot recommended (bone scan, CT, PSMA PET)
Extra testsConsider tumor genomic classifier (e.g., Decipher) if it would change surveillance vs treatment
ConfirmatoryMRI ± repeat biopsy for surveillance candidates
Staging imagingBone imaging and pelvic ± abdominal imaging (CT or MRI), or PSMA PET/CT
Extra testsConsider a genomic classifier to guide ADT
Staging imagingBone + pelvic/abdominal imaging, or PSMA PET/CT
GeneticsGermline testing recommended
OtherBaseline testosterone, bone health (DEXA) and cardiovascular risk before long-term ADT
ImagingPSMA PET/CT or CT/MRI + bone scan to map all disease; count bone mets for volume
GeneticsGermline + somatic tumor testing (HRR genes like BRCA2/ATM, MSI/dMMR, TMB)
LabsTestosterone (castration = <50 ng/dL), alkaline phosphatase, CBC

AJCC Staging Tables

The AJCC 8th edition definitions, as used in the NCCN guidelines.

T1a / T1bIncidental in ≤5% / >5% of resected tissue
T1cIdentified by needle biopsy (not palpable)
T2a / T2b / T2cPalpable, confined: ≤half of one side / >half of one side / both sides
T3aExtraprostatic extension (unilateral or bilateral)
T3bSeminal vesicle invasion

There is no pT1. Margin status (R0/R1) is reported separately.

High-Yield Summary
  • The workup goes in order: PSA and DRE, MRI, targeted plus systematic biopsy, Gleason score and Grade Group, T stage, risk group, and then staging imaging if needed.
  • Gleason 3+3 is Grade Group 1, 3+4 is Grade Group 2, 4+3 is Grade Group 3, a score of 8 is Grade Group 4, and 9 to 10 is Grade Group 5.
  • Clinical T stage comes from the DRE, with T3a for extraprostatic extension and T3b for seminal vesicle invasion.
  • Intermediate-risk features are T2b to T2c, Grade Group 2 to 3, or PSA 10 to 20, and high-risk features are T3a, Grade Group 4 to 5, or PSA over 20.
  • Staging imaging (PSMA PET, or CT plus bone scan) starts at unfavorable intermediate risk.

Treatment Paradigms.title: Prostate Cancer Treatment Paradigms
Treatment Paradigms.html:
This page answers: what does this patient's risk actually mean for radiation? Risk group establishes the treatment framework. The final plan depends on life expectancy, urinary function, anatomy, patient preference, local extent, nodal risk, imaging, and whether the patient has already undergone surgery or systemic therapy.

1
Risk group → treatment options

Which options are reasonable at all: surveillance, surgery, radiation, and whether ADT belongs in the plan.

2
Patient selection

Life expectancy, baseline urinary and sexual function, gland size, prior surgery, and what the patient values.

3
Radiation strategy

What to treat (prostate ± SVs ± nodes), how (EBRT, SBRT, brachy), and what to add (ADT, intensification).

The Full Radiation Oncology Workflow

Prostate is the cleanest disease site to see a patient go all the way through radiation oncology. This is the spine of the whole module:

1
PSA → MRI → biopsy / Grade Group
→
2
NCCN risk ± PSMA PET
→
3
RT vs surgery vs surveillance
→
4
Prostate ± SVs ± pelvic nodes
5
IMRT/VMAT, SBRT, or brachy
→
6
Protect rectum, bladder, urethra, bowel
→
7
PSA response
→
8
Salvage if recurrence

Paradigm 1: Localized Disease

Localized disease by risk group

A framework, not a prescription. Life expectancy and patient factors decide between the options.

1
If the risk group is…
Very low or low
Active surveillance for most; definitive treatment for selected patients.
2
If the risk group is…
Favorable intermediate
Definitive local therapy (EBRT, SBRT, brachy, or prostatectomy), generally without ADT; surveillance in selected patients.
3
If the risk group is…
Unfavorable intermediate
RT + short-term ADT (or EBRT + brachy boost), or prostatectomy.
4
If the risk group is…
High or very high
Dose-escalated RT + long-term ADT, ± pelvic nodes, ± brachy boost, ± systemic intensification; or surgery in selected patients.

Very Low and Low Risk: Active Surveillance

Active surveillance is active management, not "doing nothing." The cancer is followed closely with a plan to treat for cure if it changes.

1
Regular PSA
→
2
Repeat MRI
→
3
Repeat biopsy
→
4
Treat if reclassified or progressing
Active surveillance
Curative intent, deferred

Scheduled PSA, MRI, and biopsy. Treat with curative intent if the cancer upgrades. About half of men are eventually treated, without a survival cost (ProtecT).

Watchful waiting
No curative plan

For men with limited life expectancy. No scheduled biopsies; treat symptoms if they appear.

Definitive treatment may be chosen instead for a younger man with higher-volume GG1, a concerning MRI or genomic result, or a strong personal preference.

Favorable Intermediate: One Local Treatment

  • EBRT (moderately hypofractionated or SBRT), brachytherapy monotherapy, or radical prostatectomy are all reasonable.
  • ADT is generally omitted for favorable-intermediate-risk patients receiving definitive RT.
  • Target: the prostate ± proximal seminal vesicles. Pelvic nodes are not treated.
  • Selected men (e.g., low-volume GG2) can be on active surveillance.

Unfavorable Intermediate: ADT Enters the Picture

The jump from favorable to unfavorable intermediate is clinically important because ADT enters the radiation treatment paradigm.
  • EBRT + short-term ADT (about 4–6 months; RTOG 9408).
  • Or EBRT + brachytherapy boost (± ADT): better biochemical control than dose-escalated EBRT, with more urinary toxicity (ASCENDE-RT).
  • Or prostatectomy + pelvic node dissection.
  • Pelvic nodes are generally not treated at this risk level.

High and Very High Risk

1
Start ADT
→
2
About 2–3 months later: dose-escalated RT to prostate + SVs ± pelvic nodes
→
3
Continue long-term ADT (18–36 months)
  • Long-term ADT: longer ADT beat short ADT for high-risk disease (RTOG 9202, EORTC 22961).
  • Brachytherapy boost is an option for dose escalation in fit patients with suitable anatomy.
  • Surgery is an option for selected men, often followed by RT if pathology is adverse.

Pelvic nodes. Pelvic nodal treatment is considered when the estimated risk of occult nodal disease is sufficiently high, with imaging and clinical factors incorporated into the decision. In POP-RT, high-risk patients with a substantial estimated nodal risk had better biochemical and disease-free survival with whole-pelvis RT than with prostate-only RT. Risk group alone doesn't draw the field.

Treatment Intensification Beyond ADT

Selected high-risk/very-high-risk or node-positive patients may receive systemic treatment intensification beyond ADT based on contemporary evidence and guidelines. The best-known example: in STAMPEDE, adding abiraterone to ADT and RT improved metastasis-free and overall survival for high-risk nonmetastatic disease meeting specific criteria. It is not simply the next rung for everyone with high-risk disease.

Try it: cT1c, Gleason 4+3, PSA 6, healthy 68-year-old who prefers radiation. What framework?▾

Unfavorable intermediate (GG3). Radiation would generally be paired with short-term ADT, or given as EBRT + brachy boost. Prostatectomy is the alternative.

The Tools: Surgery, External Beam, Brachytherapy, and ADT

Surgery: Radical Prostatectomy

  • Removes the prostate and seminal vesicles (usually robotic), with a pelvic lymph node dissection for higher-risk disease.
  • More early incontinence and erectile dysfunction than RT; few bowel effects.
  • Gives full pathology (pT, margins, nodes) and a PSA that should become undetectable.
  • ProtecT: surgery, RT + short ADT, and active monitoring had similar, very high prostate cancer survival at 15 years in mostly low- and intermediate-risk men. They differ in side effects.

External Beam: How Many Fractions?

Prostate cancer is thought to have a relatively low α/β ratio, providing a radiobiologic rationale for hypofractionation: larger fraction sizes can maintain tumor control while allowing substantially shorter treatment courses. Trials then confirmed it clinically.

ApproachRepresentative regimenEvidence
ConventionalLong course: about 78 Gy in 39 fractions (8 weeks)Dose-escalation trials
Moderate hypofractionationAbout 20–28 fractions, e.g., 60 Gy in 20CHHiP: noninferior to conventional
SBRTAbout 5 fractions, e.g., 36.25 Gy in 5PACE-B: noninferior for low and intermediate risk
BrachytherapyInternal high-dose treatment, alone or as a boostASCENDE-RT (boost)

What Actually Happens During Prostate Brachytherapy?

Brachytherapy places the radiation source inside or immediately adjacent to the prostate, allowing a very high prostate dose while exploiting rapid dose fall-off outside the target.

LDR (permanent seeds)
Seeds stay in
  • Lithotomy, transrectal ultrasound in the rectum
  • A template grid against the perineum guides the needles
  • Seeds (e.g., I-125) are deposited along each needle
  • Real-time imaging with prostate, urethra, and rectum contoured
  • Post-implant CT checks the dosimetry
HDR (temporary source)
Source comes and goes
  • Catheters placed through the perineum into the prostate, under TRUS
  • Plan built on the catheter positions
  • A single radioactive source temporarily dwells at points within each catheter
  • Catheters are removed after treatment; nothing stays in the patient

Who suits brachy: a gland that is not too large, no large prior TURP defect, and good baseline urinary function. The TRUS view you'll see in the suite is in Imaging.

ADT: What Is It Actually Doing?

1
Prostate cancer depends on androgen receptor signaling
→
2
ADT lowers testosterone
→
3
Tumor growth is suppressed
→
4
RT works better locally, and occult disease is controlled
Setting (with RT)ADT
Low / favorable intermediateGenerally none
Unfavorable intermediateShort-term, about 4–6 months
High / very high, N1Long-term, about 18–36 months
  • GnRH agonist (leuprolide; an antiandrogen first blocks the testosterone flare) or antagonist (degarelix, oral relugolix; no flare).
  • Usually starts before RT (shrinks the gland) and continues during and after.
  • Side effects: hot flashes, fatigue, low libido, bone loss, weight gain, metabolic and cardiovascular risk, mood changes.
ADT is a radiation partner. It is not routinely added to prostatectomy for localized disease.

Paradigm 2: Node-Positive Disease (cN1)

Pelvic nodes on PSMA PET or CT with no distant disease is stage IVA but still treated for cure.

  • RT to the prostate + pelvic nodes, with a boost to the involved nodes while respecting bowel.
  • Long-term ADT, with systemic intensification (e.g., abiraterone, STAMPEDE) for appropriate patients.
  • Surgery + extended pelvic node dissection is an option for selected patients.
High risk, N0
Nodes at risk

Elective pelvis when nodal risk is high enough, prostate to full dose, long-term ADT.

N1
Nodes involved

Elective pelvis plus a boost to the involved nodes, prostate to full dose, long-term ADT ± intensification.

Paradigm 3: After Prostatectomy

After surgery the PSA should become undetectable. A rising PSA is how most recurrences show up, often years before any scan finding.

1
PSA undetectable → PSA surveillance
→
2
PSA becomes detectable / rises
→
3
PSMA PET ± MRI
→
4
Early salvage RT: prostate bed ± pelvic nodes
→
5
Add ADT when recurrence-risk features justify it
Adverse pathology, PSA undetectable
Usually observe
  • Positive margin, pT3a/pT3b
  • RADICALS-RT, RAVES, GETUG-AFU 17: early salvage gave outcomes similar to routine adjuvant RT, and many men never needed RT
  • Adjuvant RT is still considered for selected very high-risk pathology (e.g., pN1)
PSA rising
Early salvage RT
  • Treat early: outcomes are better at lower PSA
  • Prostate bed to about 64–66 Gy
  • PSMA PET can add PET-positive pelvic nodes to the plan
  • Risk-adapted ADT and pelvic nodes for higher-risk recurrences (RTOG 9601, SPPORT)
A Negative PSMA PET Is Not a Reason to Wait

A negative PSMA PET does not mean you should withhold salvage prostate-bed RT when the clinical indication for salvage RT is present. Early recurrences are often too small to see, and salvage works best at low PSA. (AUA/ASTRO/SUO salvage guideline, 2024.)

  • Biochemical recurrence: after surgery, a detectable PSA that rises (classically >0.2, confirmed); after RT, nadir + 2 (Phoenix).
  • PSA doubling time: a short doubling time suggests a more aggressive recurrence and a higher chance of distant disease.
  • RTOG 9601 nuance: the survival benefit of adding ADT was concentrated in men with higher PSA at salvage; at very low PSA the benefit is small, which is why ADT is risk-adapted.
Try it: 2 years after prostatectomy (pT3a, GG3, margin negative), PSA is 0.25 then 0.38. PSMA PET negative. Plan?▾

Early salvage RT to the prostate bed. The negative PET doesn't change the indication. Consider short-term ADT and pelvic nodes given GG3/pT3a and a rising PSA (SPPORT).

Paradigm 4: Metastatic Disease

Hormone-sensitive (mHSPC)
ADT + treatment intensification
  • ADT + an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (abiraterone, enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide) ± docetaxel
  • Prostate RT for selected de novo low-volume disease (STAMPEDE)
Castration-resistant (mCRPC)
Progression despite castrate testosterone
  • Change systemic therapy based on prior treatment, molecular profile, PSMA expression, symptoms, and disease distribution
  • Options include taxanes, PARP inhibitors (repair-gene mutations), radium-223 (bone-only), and Lu-177 PSMA (PSMA-positive)

Where Radiation Fits

SituationRadiation role
De novo low-volume mHSPCRT to the prostate in selected patients
Selected oligometastatic diseaseSBRT to each site (often on a trial)
Painful bone metastasisPalliative RT; 8 Gy × 1 relieves pain as well as longer courses
Spinal cord compressionUrgent: steroids, MRI of the whole spine, surgery if appropriate, and RT

How a Prostate RT Plan Is Built

1. Simulation

Bladder preparation, rectal preparation, immobilization, fiducials when used, a planning CT, and MRI fusion (step by step in Imaging). The aim is a prostate that sits in the same place every day.

2. Targets: Intact Prostate

PTVThe CTVs plus a margin for daily setup and motion; smaller when image guidance is good
Elective nodal CTV (when indicated)Pelvic nodes for higher-risk or node-positive disease; lower dose
CTVThe prostate ± seminal vesicles (how much SV depends on risk); full dose
MRI-visible lesionSometimes boosted to a higher dose (FLAME)
While protecting
  • Rectum
  • Bladder
  • Urethra
  • Penile bulb
  • Small bowel / sigmoid
  • Femoral heads

After prostatectomy, the CTV is the prostate bed (± pelvic nodes), drawn from a consensus atlas because there is no gland left to see.

3. Image Guidance

The prostate moves relative to the bony pelvis as the bladder and rectum fill. Daily cone-beam CT, fiducial imaging, or MRI guidance lets the team align to the prostate itself, which is what makes tight margins and SBRT possible.

4. Techniques

IMRT / VMAT

The standard for external beam: shapes dose around the prostate and away from rectum and bladder.

SBRT

Five or so large, highly conformal fractions; depends on excellent image guidance.

Brachytherapy

Sources inside the gland; very high dose with rapid fall-off.

Toxicity: What Patients Feel, and When

Acute
During RT and the weeks after
  • GU: frequency, urgency, weak stream, dysuria
  • GI: loose stool, urgency, rectal irritation
  • Fatigue
  • Managed with alpha-blockers (e.g., tamsulosin) and antidiarrheals
Late
Months to years
  • GU: hematuria, urethral stricture, persistent urinary dysfunction
  • GI: rectal bleeding, proctitis
  • Sexual: erectile dysfunction
  • A small risk of second cancers (bladder, rectum)
Baseline urinary and sexual function matters because treatment toxicity is experienced on top of the patient's pre-treatment function.

The Evidence: One Trial per Clinical Question

ProtecT

Can low-risk disease be monitored? Monitoring, surgery, and RT + short ADT had similar prostate cancer survival at 15 years; they differ in side effects.

RTOG 9408

Does ADT add benefit to RT? Short-term ADT with RT improved survival, mainly in intermediate risk.

RTOG 9202 / EORTC 22961

Does high-risk disease need longer ADT? Yes: long-term ADT beat short-term.

CHHiP / PACE-B

Can RT be shorter? 60 Gy in 20 and 36.25 Gy in 5 were noninferior to longer courses.

ASCENDE-RT

Is a brachy boost more effective? Better biochemical control than dose-escalated EBRT, with more urinary toxicity and no survival difference.

POP-RT

Should we treat the pelvis? Whole-pelvis RT improved biochemical and disease-free survival in high-risk patients with substantial nodal risk.

RADICALS / RAVES / GETUG-AFU 17

Adjuvant or early salvage? Early salvage gave similar outcomes and spared many men RT.

RTOG 9601 / SPPORT

Should ADT be added to salvage RT? ADT improved outcomes (more so at higher PSA); pelvic nodes + ADT improved freedom from progression.

STAMPEDE

Systemic intensification? Abiraterone helped selected high-risk M0/N1 disease; prostate RT helped low-volume metastatic disease.

High-Yield Summary
  • Very low and low-risk disease gets active surveillance.
  • Favorable intermediate risk gets RT alone or prostatectomy, with no ADT.
  • Unfavorable intermediate risk gets RT plus 4 to 6 months of ADT, and high or very high risk gets RT plus 18 to 36 months of ADT with pelvic nodal RT.
  • After prostatectomy, early salvage RT to the prostate bed when the PSA starts rising is as effective as routine adjuvant RT and spares many men treatment.
  • Prostate cancer has a low alpha/beta ratio, so hypofractionated and SBRT courses work well.
